title: SCADA
summary: SCADA, short for supervisory control and data acquisition, is the layer of an industrial control environment that gives operators a consolidated view of many remote sites and lets them issue supervisory commands. A typical system is a control centre with operator screens, a historian, and a set of remote terminal units or programmable logic controllers in the field, communicating over protocols such as Modbus or DNP3 that were designed for reliability rather than for security. It is used where assets are spread over distance, such as power distribution, water treatment, pipelines and rail. The mistake that recurs is to secure the corporate network carefully and then treat the control network as invisible, since flat control networks, shared accounts and unlogged remote vendor access mean that one compromised engineering workstation can reach every controller on the site.

beginner.definition: SCADA means supervisory control and data acquisition. It is a system that lets operators watch and control equipment spread over a wide area. It collects readings from sensors and shows them on screens. It also sends commands, such as opening a valve or starting a pump.
beginner.whyItMatters: SCADA systems run things that people depend on, such as water and electricity. A mistake or an attack can stop a service or damage equipment. Many of these systems were built for reliability, not for security. They often last for decades and cannot be patched quickly. Protecting them needs care, because downtime can be dangerous on its own.
howItWorks: Field devices measure the process, such as flow or pressure, and store the values locally.
Remote terminal units send those readings to the control centre over a communications link.
The control centre shows the data on operator screens and records it in a historian.
Operators send supervisory commands back to the field devices when a change is needed.
Local controllers keep running their own logic if the link to the centre is lost.
Engineers connect with laptops for maintenance, which is a common weak point to control.
beginner.example: Think of a large farm with many fields and one farmhouse. Sensors in each field report soil and water levels. The farmhouse shows all of them on one board, and the farmer decides where to open the irrigation gates. Workers in the fields can still act alone if the radio fails. SCADA is the farmhouse board, the radio link, and the workers in the fields together.
takeaways: SCADA is the supervisory layer that watches and commands remote industrial equipment.
These networks are flat and long lived, so assume that built in security is weak.
Remote maintenance access is one of the most valuable paths to protect.

objectives: Explain what SCADA means and which parts make up a SCADA system.
Describe how field data reaches the control centre and how commands return.
Explain why industrial protocols often lack strong security features.
Identify the risks created by remote access and flat control networks.
Outline how segmentation and monitoring protect a control environment.
